How to Help Your Child Think Creatively with AI Without Letting AI Do the Thinking

Three practical tips for parents: think first, create boldly, use AI wisely. Plus what AkiliNest does differently in creative programmes for children aged 8-17.

If your child reaches for ChatGPT before they reach for a pencil, you are not alone. Nairobi parents tell us the same worry: AI is everywhere, but original thinking feels harder to protect. The goal is not to ban technology. It is to make sure your child leads with their own mind, then uses AI as a tool, not a shortcut.

Before any screen opens, ask one question: what do you think? Whether it is homework, a story idea, or a weekend project, give your child 60 seconds of silence to form an opinion. Research on cognitive offloading shows that skipping this step trains children to outsource judgment. A simple habit at home: no AI until they can explain their idea in one sentence aloud.

Creativity needs friction. Drawing, building, debating, and presenting all force the brain to connect ideas. Nairobi families often fill weekends with passive screen time because it is easy. Swap one hour for making: a comic, a cardboard prototype, a short video they storyboard first. The product matters less than the process of deciding, revising, and owning the result.

When AI enters, set a rule: it suggests, you decide. Children can use AI to brainstorm titles, check spelling, or explore examples, but they must mark what came from them versus the machine. Parents who model this (I asked AI for options, then I picked the one I disagreed with) teach discernment better than any lecture on cheating.
